title: Run a meeting, don't "do" it
rule: Meetings are run or led, not done.

examples.work: I ran today's stand-up because Priya was on leave.
examples.everyday: My brother led the planning for Mum's birthday dinner.

insteadOf: I did the meeting today.
analogy: A captain leads the team; nobody says the captain "did" the match.
tryPrompt: You were in charge of the client call this morning. Say it in one sentence.
answer: I ran the client call this morning.

title: Make changes, not "do" changes
rule: You make changes; you don't do them.

examples.work: I made a few changes to the deck after your comments.
examples.everyday: Mum made a few changes to the Diwali menu this year.

insteadOf: I did some changes in the deck.
analogy: A tailor makes changes to your shirt; he doesn't "do" them.
tryPrompt: You edited the report after feedback. Tell your manager in one sentence.
answer: I've made the changes you suggested.

title: Say what you found and fixed
rule: Name the result: found, fixed, solved. Not just "looked into".

examples.work: I found the cause: a wrong date format. It's fixed now.
examples.everyday: The fan was making a noise. I fixed it with one screw.

insteadOf: I looked into the issue.
analogy: A mechanic says "I fixed the brakes", not "I looked into your car".
tryPrompt: You solved a login bug today. Tell your team what you did in one sentence.
answer: I fixed the login bug. It was a wrong setting.

title: Flag a problem early
rule: "Flag" means point out a problem so others notice it.

examples.work: I want to flag a risk: the vendor hasn't replied yet.
examples.everyday: My sister flagged that our train tickets were for the wrong date.

insteadOf: I just wanted to inform one issue.
analogy: Like a railway guard waving a flag: a signal that something needs attention now.
tryPrompt: You notice the launch date clashes with Diwali. How do you raise it early in the meeting?
answer: I'd like to flag something: the launch date clashes with Diwali.

title: Approve: an official yes
rule: "Approve" means you officially say yes to something.

examples.work: Rahul approved the design, so we can start on Monday.
examples.everyday: Dad approved the road trip as long as I drive.

insteadOf: My leave got passed by the manager.
analogy: Approving is the signal turning green: now the train can go.
tryPrompt: Your manager said yes to your leave request. Tell your team in one sentence.
answer: My manager approved my leave for next week.

title: Make a mistake
rule: Mistakes are made, not done.

examples.work: I made a mistake in the invoice; I'll send a corrected one.
examples.everyday: Everyone makes mistakes when they're learning to drive.

insteadOf: I did a mistake in the invoice.
analogy: Words come in pairs, like chai and biscuit: "make" goes with "mistake".
tryPrompt: You sent the wrong file to a client. Admit it in one sentence.
answer: Sorry, I made a mistake and sent the wrong file.

title: Raise a concern
rule: To raise a concern is to say you're worried about something.

examples.work: Arjun raised a concern about the testing time.
examples.everyday: Mum raised a concern about me driving home late at night.

insteadOf: I want to put one concern.
analogy: Like raising your hand in class: you lift the worry so everyone sees it.
tryPrompt: You think two weeks is too little for testing. Say it politely in the meeting.
answer: Can I raise a concern? Two weeks feels tight for testing.

title: Heavy traffic
rule: Traffic is heavy or light, not big or small.

examples.work: Sorry I'm late. There was heavy traffic on the ring road.
examples.everyday: Leave early on Friday; the traffic to Pune is always heavy.

insteadOf: There was big traffic today.
analogy: Picture a heavy bag on your back: that's how a jammed road feels.
tryPrompt: You're joining the call ten minutes late because of the roads. Message your team.
answer: Running ten minutes late, sorry. Heavy traffic on the way.

title: Make a decision
rule: "Make a decision" works everywhere; British people also say "take".

examples.work: We need to make a decision on the vendor by Friday.
examples.everyday: We finally made a decision: Goa for the long weekend.

analogy: Like choosing a train at the junction: once you make the decision, you're moving.
tryPrompt: Your team keeps discussing two designs. Ask them to choose one today.
answer: Can we make a decision on the design today?

title: Strong coffee, strong chai
rule: Coffee and tea are strong or weak, not powerful.

examples.work: I need a strong coffee before this 9 a.m. client call.
examples.everyday: Make my chai strong, please, with less sugar.

insteadOf: This chai is very powerful.
analogy: Strong chai is like a firm handshake: you really feel it.
tryPrompt: At a café, you want coffee with more taste and less milk. Ask for it.
answer: Could I get a strong coffee, please?

title: "Do the needful" → name the action
rule: In global English, name the exact action you need.

examples.work: Please approve the invoice by Friday.
examples.everyday: Could you pick up the cake on your way home?

insteadOf: Please do the needful.
analogy: Like telling an auto driver "go" versus giving him the address.
tryPrompt: You need IT to reset your laptop password. Ask them clearly in one line.
answer: Could you please reset my laptop password today?

title: "I have a doubt" → "a question"
rule: In global English, say "I have a question", not "a doubt".

examples.work: Quick question about the timeline: is it the end of May?
examples.everyday: Quick question: does this train stop at Thane?

insteadOf: Sir, I have a doubt about the timeline.
analogy: Abroad, "a doubt" can sound like a third-umpire review: you think they got it wrong.
tryPrompt: In a training session, you didn't understand step three. Ask the trainer.
answer: Sorry, I have a question about step three.

title: "Discuss about" → "discuss"
rule: In global English, "discuss" already means "talk about"; drop "about".

examples.work: Let's discuss the plan tomorrow after stand-up.
examples.everyday: We discussed the wedding menu over chai.

insteadOf: Let's discuss about the plan tomorrow.
analogy: Saying "discuss about" is like ordering "chai tea": the second word repeats the first.
tryPrompt: You want to talk through the new design with Riya. Invite her.
answer: Riya, can we discuss the new design this afternoon?

title: "Today itself" → "by end of day"
rule: In global English, say "by end of day", not "today itself".

examples.work: I'll send the report by end of day.
examples.everyday: I'll book the tickets today, before they sell out.

insteadOf: I'll send the report today itself.
analogy: Like a courier promising "by 6 p.m.": a clear time beats extra emphasis.
tryPrompt: Your manager needs the slides urgently. Promise them today, clearly.
answer: I'll send the slides by end of day today.

title: "The below" → "below"
rule: In global English, put "below" after the noun: "the file below".

examples.work: Please check the numbers in the table below.
examples.everyday: The recipe below serves four, so double it for Diwali.

insteadOf: Please see the below table.
analogy: Like a lift sign, "Parking below": the place first, then the direction.
tryPrompt: In an email, you want people to read the steps listed underneath. Write that line.
answer: Please follow the steps below.

title: "Passed out" → "graduated"
rule: In global English, say "graduated"; "passed out" means "fainted".

examples.work: I graduated in 2019 and started here as a junior designer.
examples.everyday: My sister graduated from Pune University last month.

insteadOf: I passed out of college in 2019.
analogy: Say "passed out" abroad and people picture you fainting at the convocation.
tryPrompt: A new colleague asks about your college. Say when you finished your degree.
answer: I graduated in 2019, from an engineering college in Nagpur.

title: "Out of station" → "out of town"
rule: In global English, say "out of town", not "out of station".

examples.work: I'll be out of town Monday to Wednesday; Rahul will cover.
examples.everyday: We're out of town for Onam, back on Sunday.

insteadOf: I'll be out of station next week.
analogy: "Station" makes people picture a train platform; "town" tells them you've left the city.
tryPrompt: You'll miss Thursday's meeting because you're travelling home. Tell the team.
answer: I'll be out of town on Thursday, so I'll miss the meeting.

title: "Cousin brother" → "cousin"
rule: In global English, "cousin" alone works for both boys and girls.

examples.work: Can I leave at four? My cousin is landing from Dubai.
examples.everyday: My cousin and I watched the match at his place.

insteadOf: My cousin brother is visiting this weekend.
analogy: "Cousin" is like "teammate": one word fits everyone, boy or girl.
tryPrompt: A colleague asks who you spent Diwali with. Mention your male cousin.
answer: I spent Diwali with my cousin and his family.

title: "Shifting house" → "moving house"
rule: In global English, say "moving house", not "shifting house".

examples.work: Can I work from home on Friday? We're moving house.
examples.everyday: We're moving to a bigger flat near my office.

insteadOf: I'm shifting house this weekend.
analogy: Even the trucks say "Packers and Movers": you're moving house, not shifting it.
tryPrompt: Tell your manager you need Friday off to move to a new flat.
answer: Could I take Friday off? We're moving house.

title: "Myself Arjun" → "I'm Arjun"
rule: In global English, start with "I'm", not "Myself".

examples.work: Hi everyone, I'm Arjun, from the design team.
examples.everyday: Hi, I'm Fatima, Riya's friend from school.

insteadOf: Myself Arjun, from the design team.
analogy: "I'm" is a handshake; "Myself" sounds like reading from a form.
tryPrompt: You join a call with a new client team. Introduce yourself in one line.
answer: Hi, I'm Arjun. I lead design on this project.

title: "Informations" → "information"
rule: In global English, "information" never takes an -s.

examples.work: Could you share more information about the new process?
examples.everyday: The station app has all the information on train timings.

insteadOf: Please share the informations.
analogy: Information is like rice: you ask for more rice, never "rices".
tryPrompt: You need details about tomorrow's offsite. Ask HR in one line.
answer: Could you send me some information about tomorrow's offsite?

title: "Feedbacks" → "feedback"
rule: In global English, say "some feedback", never "feedbacks".

examples.work: Thanks for the feedback; I'll update the slides today.
examples.everyday: I asked my friends for feedback on my biryani.

insteadOf: Thanks for all the feedbacks.
analogy: Feedback is like traffic: there can be a lot of it, never "many traffics".
tryPrompt: Your team reviewed your design. Thank them in one line.
answer: Thanks, everyone, for the feedback on my design.

title: "Luggages" → "luggage" or "bags"
rule: In global English, "luggage" has no plural; count "bags" instead.

examples.work: Leave your luggage at reception; the meeting room is small.
examples.everyday: We've got three bags, so we'll need a bigger cab.

insteadOf: I have three luggages.
analogy: Luggage is the whole pile on the trolley; bags are what you count.
tryPrompt: A hotel porter asks how much you are carrying. You have two suitcases. Answer.
answer: Just two bags, thanks.

title: "Equipments" → "equipment"
rule: In global English, "equipment" and "furniture" never take an -s.

examples.work: The new studio equipment arrives on Monday.
examples.everyday: We bought some furniture for the new flat.

insteadOf: We need new equipments for the studio.
analogy: Equipment is the whole cricket kit; bats and pads are what you count.
tryPrompt: You need two more laptops and a projector for a training day. Ask IT.
answer: Could we get some more equipment for the training: two laptops and a projector?

title: "A good news" → "some good news"
rule: In global English, "news" takes no "a": say "some good news".

examples.work: I have some good news: the client signed today.
examples.everyday: Great news! Riya got into her dream college.

insteadOf: I have a good news!
analogy: Need just one? Say "a piece of news", like one slice from a whole cake.
tryPrompt: Your project just got approved. Tell your team in one line.
answer: I've got some good news: our project was approved!

title: Bring forward
rule: "Bring forward" means move something to an earlier time.

examples.work: Can we bring the call forward to 3?
examples.everyday: We brought the trip forward so we'd be home for Onam.

insteadOf: Can we prepone the call?
analogy: Like pulling a chair closer: you bring the date nearer to today.
tryPrompt: The client wants Friday's demo on Wednesday. Ask your team if that's possible.
answer: Can we bring the demo forward to Wednesday?

title: Push back
rule: "Push back" means move something to a later time.

examples.work: Can we push the meeting back an hour? I'm stuck in traffic.
examples.everyday: We pushed dinner back to nine because Dad's train was late.

insteadOf: Can we make the meeting late by one hour?
analogy: Like pushing your plate back: same plate, just further away.
tryPrompt: Your report needs two more days. Ask your manager for a later deadline.
answer: Could we push the deadline back to Thursday?

title: Follow up
rule: "Follow up" means check back later on something already started.

examples.work: I'll follow up with the vendor tomorrow if they don't reply.
examples.everyday: I'll follow up with the plumber about the leaking tap.

insteadOf: I'll ask again regarding the same.
analogy: Like a fielder chasing the ball after it's hit: you keep going after it.
tryPrompt: You'll check with the client again on Monday. Tell your manager in one line.
answer: I'll follow up with the client on Monday.

title: Sort out
rule: "Sort out" means fix a problem or put something in order.

examples.work: Give me an hour; I'll sort out the login issue.
examples.everyday: Can you sort out the Wi-Fi? It keeps dropping.

insteadOf: I'll do something about the issue.
analogy: Like sorting a messy drawer: you're done when everything's in its place.
tryPrompt: A teammate's laptop won't connect to the office network. Say you'll fix it.
answer: Don't worry, I'll sort it out in ten minutes.

title: Run into a problem
rule: "Run into" a problem means meet it unexpectedly.

examples.work: We ran into a bug on the checkout page this morning.
examples.everyday: We ran into heavy traffic near Silk Board.

analogy: Like an auto turning a corner and finding a cow in the road.
tryPrompt: Testing is late because of a server issue nobody expected. Tell your manager.
answer: We ran into a server issue, so testing is a day behind.

title: Catch up
rule: "Catch up" means talk and share news after some time apart.

examples.work: Let's catch up after your leave. I want to hear about the trip.
examples.everyday: Let's catch up this weekend; it's been months!

analogy: Like checking the score after missing a few overs: you catch up on what happened.
tryPrompt: You haven't spoken to an old colleague in a while. Suggest coffee to talk.
answer: It's been ages! Want to catch up over coffee this week?

title: Fill someone in
rule: "Fill someone in" means tell them what they missed.

examples.work: I missed the stand-up. Can you fill me in?
examples.everyday: Fill me in: what happened at the party?

insteadOf: Can you update me what happened?
analogy: Like filling the blanks in a form: they give you the missing parts.
tryPrompt: You were on leave yesterday and missed a meeting. Ask Rahul what happened.
answer: Rahul, could you fill me in on yesterday's meeting?

title: Set up a meeting
rule: "Set up" a meeting means arrange it.

examples.work: I'll set up a call with the client for Tuesday.
examples.everyday: Let's set up a video call with Grandma on Sunday.

analogy: Like setting up the stumps before a match: you get everything ready to play.
tryPrompt: You need 30 minutes with the design team next week. Offer to arrange it.
answer: I'll set up a 30-minute call with design next week.

title: Go over
rule: "Go over" something means check or review it carefully.

examples.work: Can we go over the numbers before the client call?
examples.everyday: Let's go over the packing list before we leave.

analogy: Like running your finger down a shopping list before leaving the kirana shop.
tryPrompt: You want Priya to check the slides with you before tomorrow's pitch. Ask her.
answer: Priya, can we go over the slides before tomorrow's pitch?

title: Point out
rule: "Point out" means show someone something they may have missed.

examples.work: Joseph pointed out a typo on the first slide.
examples.everyday: My friend pointed out we were on the wrong platform.

analogy: Like a friend tapping your shoulder and pointing: "Look, your train's here."
tryPrompt: In a review, you notice the date on slide 4 is wrong. Mention it politely.
answer: Can I point out one thing? The date on slide 4 is wrong.

title: "Just to recap…"
rule: Use "Just to recap" to sum up before a meeting ends.

examples.work: Just to recap: Riya builds it, I test it, launch Friday.
examples.everyday: Just to recap: you buy snacks, I bring the speaker.

analogy: Like the highlights at the end of a match: the key moments, fast.
tryPrompt: The meeting is ending. Sum up the two next steps for the team.
answer: Just to recap: Arjun sends the quote, and I'll book the room.

title: "Can we park that?"
rule: "Can we park that?" means let's leave it for later.

examples.work: Good point, but can we park that until next week?
examples.everyday: Can we park the holiday plan till after exams?

analogy: Like parking a car: it's safe, it's not going anywhere, you'll come back.
tryPrompt: Someone raises a new topic, but time is short. Suggest leaving it for later.
answer: Good point. Can we park that and come back to it on Friday?

title: "Can I add something?"
rule: Ask "Can I add something?" to join in politely.

examples.work: Can I add something? The client also wants a Hindi version.
examples.everyday: Can I add something? The restaurant shuts at ten, so let's hurry.

insteadOf: Sorry to disturb, one point from my side.
analogy: Like waiting for a gap in traffic before you merge in.
tryPrompt: Your team is planning dates, and you know a holiday clashes. Join in politely.
answer: Can I add something? Diwali falls that week, so many people will be off.

title: "So the next step is…"
rule: End with "So the next step is…" and name who does what.

examples.work: So the next step is: Fatima shares the draft by Thursday.
examples.everyday: So the next step is: I book the tickets, you pack.

analogy: Like the guard's whistle at the station: everyone knows what happens next.
tryPrompt: The call is ending. Say what happens next: you'll send the plan tomorrow.
answer: So the next step is: I'll send the plan tomorrow.

title: "Let's pick this up tomorrow."
rule: "Let's pick this up tomorrow" means continue it later.

examples.work: We're out of time. Let's pick this up tomorrow at ten.
examples.everyday: It's late and we're all tired. Let's pick this up after breakfast.

analogy: Like pausing a film at the interval: you'll start right where you stopped.
tryPrompt: The discussion is running late. Suggest continuing on Monday morning.
answer: We're out of time. Let's pick this up on Monday morning.

title: "I'll get back to you by…"
rule: Say "I'll get back to you by" and give a time.

examples.work: Let me check with the team; I'll get back to you by Friday.
examples.everyday: Let me check with Mum and get back to you tonight.

insteadOf: I'll check and tell.
analogy: Like a train timetable: people relax when they know the time, not just "soon".
tryPrompt: A client asks a question you can't answer yet. Promise a reply by Wednesday.
answer: Good question. Let me check and get back to you by Wednesday.

title: "Thanks for flagging this."
rule: Say "Thanks for flagging this" when someone points out a problem.

examples.work: Thanks for flagging this, Rahul. I'll fix it today.
examples.everyday: Thanks for flagging that the gas cylinder's nearly empty!

analogy: Like thanking the person who shouts "mind the step": they saved you a fall.
tryPrompt: A teammate tells you the link in your email is broken. Thank them and promise a fix.
answer: Thanks for flagging this. I'll send the right link now.

title: "Sounds good, go ahead."
rule: "Sounds good, go ahead" gives a warm, quick yes.

examples.work: Sounds good, go ahead and send it to the client.
examples.everyday: Sounds good, go ahead and order the pizza.

insteadOf: Okay, fine, you may proceed.
analogy: Like a nod across the room: friendly, quick, and everyone knows it's a yes.
tryPrompt: A teammate asks if they can share the draft with design. Say yes warmly.
answer: Sounds good, go ahead!

title: "Leave it with me."
rule: "Leave it with me" means you'll take care of it.

examples.work: The demo link is broken? Leave it with me.
examples.everyday: Dinner needs onions? Leave it with me, back in ten.

analogy: Like handing your bags to a porter: off your hands, and in safe ones.
tryPrompt: Your manager says a client can't log in. Show you'll handle it.
answer: Leave it with me. I'll update you in 20 minutes.

title: "That's a fair point."
rule: Say "That's a fair point" to agree that someone is right.

examples.work: That's a fair point; let's test on older phones too.
examples.everyday: That's a fair point. The earlier train is less crowded.

insteadOf: Yes, yes, correct, correct.
analogy: Like a batter nodding when the umpire's right: no fuss, just a calm yes.
tryPrompt: A colleague says your plan forgets weekend traffic. They're right. Agree warmly.
answer: That's a fair point. Let's plan for weekends too.

title: "Do you have a minute?"
rule: Ask "Do you have a minute?" before starting a quick chat.

examples.work: Hi Joseph, do you have a minute? Quick question on the quote.
examples.everyday: Mum, do you have a minute? I need help with this form.

insteadOf: Ma'am, I want to talk.
analogy: Like knocking before you open a door.
tryPrompt: You need two minutes of your manager's time at her desk. Ask first.
answer: Hi, do you have a minute? I need a quick decision on the design.

title: "Could you take a look at…?"
rule: "Could you take a look at…?" asks someone to check something.

examples.work: Could you take a look at my draft before three?
examples.everyday: Could you take a look at the tap? It's still dripping.

analogy: Like handing a friend your phone: "Just see if this looks right."
tryPrompt: You want Priya to review your email before you send it. Ask her.
answer: Priya, could you take a look at this email before I send it?

title: "Would you mind…?"
rule: "Would you mind" plus an -ing verb softly asks a favour.

examples.work: Would you mind sharing your screen?
examples.everyday: Would you mind keeping my seat? I'll be right back.

insteadOf: Would you mind to send the file?
analogy: Like holding the lift door for someone: polite, small, and easy to say yes to.
tryPrompt: On a call, you want a colleague to send the file again. Ask softly.
answer: Would you mind sending the file again?

title: "When works for you?"
rule: Ask "When works for you?" so the other person picks the time.

examples.work: I need 20 minutes with you this week. When works for you?
examples.everyday: Let's meet for chai. When works for you, Saturday or Sunday?

analogy: Like letting a guest choose their chair: a small courtesy they notice.
tryPrompt: You want a call with a senior client. Let them choose the time.
answer: Could we set up a quick call? When works for you this week?

title: "Is it OK if I…?"
rule: "Is it OK if I…?" asks permission politely and simply.

examples.work: Is it OK if I join the call five minutes late?
examples.everyday: Is it OK if I bring a friend to dinner?

insteadOf: Sir, I want to leave early on Friday, please permit.
analogy: Like asking before you take the last samosa: a small check that keeps things friendly.
tryPrompt: You'd like to leave an hour early on Friday for a family event. Ask your manager.
answer: Is it OK if I leave an hour early on Friday?
